items.title: The Phases of Transcription and mRNA Processing

source_refs.note: The phases of transcription with the For Information box and post-transcriptional modifications (PDF 133-136), as printed; Figures 19.13 to 19.16 are replaced by original diagrams.

blocks.text: In this process, no primer is needed. An enzyme RNA polymerase binds at template DNA at a special nucleotides sequence. This sequence is called promoter. It is not itself transcribed by the enzyme. For example;

items: In prokaryotes, a promoter TTGACA is present 35 nucleotides before the start point of gene. So, it also called –35 sequence.
In prokaryotes, another promoter TATAAT is 10 nucleotides before the start point of gene. It is also called –10 sequence.

blocks.alt: A prokaryotic promoter on double-stranded DNA. Coding strand 5' to 3' with TTGACA at the -35 sequence, TATAAT at the -10 sequence and A at the start point; template strand 3' to 5' with the complementary AACTGT, ATATTA and T. A green arrow from 5' to 3' shows the direction of transcription.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.13: Promoters in prokaryotes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.13).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Coding strand, Template strand, -35 sequence, -10 sequence, Start point, Transcription, 5', 3'.

items: In eukaryotes, a promotor TATAAA (called TATA box) is 25 nucleotides before the start point. It is also called –25 sequence.
In eukaryotes, a promoter GGCCAATCT (called CAAT box) is 70 nucleotides before the start point. It is also called –70 sequence.

blocks.text: RNA polymerase consists of five subunits:

items: two α subunits bind with regulatory proteins,
a β′ subunit binds with template DNA,
a β subunit binds with RNA nucleotides, and
a σ subunit recognizes the promoter and initiates synthesis.

blocks.title: For Information
blocks.text: Prokaryotes have only one RNA polymerase, which synthesises all 3 kinds of RNA. Eukaryotes have three different RNA polymerases: RNA polymerase I synthesizes rRNA in the nucleolus; RNA polymerase II synthesizes mRNA; and RNA polymerase III synthesizes tRNA.

When RNA polymerase attaches to promoter, its σ subunit is removed. The other four subunits (core enzyme) catalyse the process. They unwind the DNA helix. They breakdown nucleotide-pairs (base-pairs). It results in the formation of a bubble-like structure, the transcription bubble. The assemblage of RNA chain occurs in this bubble.

Inside the transcription bubble, RNA polymerase begins making a chain of complementary ribonucleotides in front of template DNA strand. It is done in 5′ to 3′ direction. It usually starts with A or G ribonucleotide. Here, the nucleotides available for attachment are in the form of ribonucleoside triphosphates (rNTP). When an rNTP is added, its two phosphates detach with the release of energy, and ribonucleotide is attached to the chain.

The first 12 bases of new mRNA strand make a temporary helix with template DNA strand. Due to it, the position of the 3′ end of the mRNA remains stable. So, it can receive an incoming ribonucleotide. The RNA-DNA helix rotates each time a nucleotide is added. So, the 3′ end of RNA stays at the catalytic site of RNA polymerase. The transcription bubble moves down the DNA. The growing mRNA strand protrudes from the bubble. After the transcription bubble passes, the transcribed DNA is re-wound.

blocks.alt: A transcription bubble inside a pink RNA polymerase. The DNA ahead is unwinding and the DNA behind is rewinding (curved red arrows). The coding strand (yellow) loops over the top; along the template strand (blue) the new mRNA (orange) forms a short DNA-RNA hybrid helix, its 3' end growing and its 5' end leaving the enzyme. rNTPs enter the polymerase; a green arrow shows the direction of movement.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.14: Elongation phase of transcription (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.14).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Template strand, Coding strand, Rewinding, Unwinding, mRNA, DNA-RNA hybrid helix, rNTPs, RNA polymerase, 5', 3'.

blocks.text: At the end of a gene on template DNA. There is a stop codon. After this stop codon, there is a series of stop region in the form of GC nucleotide-pairs (base-pairs) followed by a series of AT pairs. When these nucleotide-pairs are transcribed into mRNA, hydrogen bonds are formed within the strand of mRNA. This intra-strand nucleotide-pairing (base-pairing) creates a loop called GC hairpin with a tail of four or more U ribonucleotides. The GC hairpin causes the RNA polymerase to pause. The pairing of four U of mRNA of with A of DNA is the weakest. It cannot hold the RNA-DNA hybrid strands together during the long pause. So, the RNA strand dissociates from DNA stand within the transcription bubble, and transcription stops.

blocks.alt: Top: RNA polymerase paused at the stop region of the DNA, the mRNA ending in UUUU paired to the stop region, and a GC hairpin formed in the mRNA behind it; an inset shows the hairpin's sequence, 5' C A then C G G C G C paired with G C C G C G, a loop G G C U U, and the 3' tail U U U U U. Below: the polymerase released, the DNA strands rewound, and the mRNA separated.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.15: Termination phase of transcription (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.15).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Polymerase paused, Stop region, GC hairpin, Polymerase released, DNA strands rewind, mRNA separates, 5', 3'.

blocks.text: As the prokaryotes have no nucleus and transcription happens in cytoplasm, their new mRNA does not need to travel anywhere to start translation. On the other hand, in eukaryotic cells the new mRNA has to travel from nucleus to cytoplasm. For this journey, the new mRNA undergoes the following modifications.

1- Addition of 5′ Cap: The first nucleotide (at the 5′ end of mRNA) is A or G. At the terminal 5′ end of A or G a methylated GTP is attached. This bond is formed between 5′end of terminal A or G and 5′end of GTP. This structure is called a 5′ cap. It protects the mRNA from nucleases and phosphatases during its journey.
2- Addition of 3′ Poly-A tail: At the 3′end of mRNA, a small chain of about 250 A nucleotides is added. It is called 3′ poly-A tail. It protects the mRNA transcript from degradation by nucleases.

blocks.alt: Template DNA 3' to 5' with a promoter and four exons separated by three introns; transcription gives the immature mRNA 5' to 3' with the same exons and introns; addition of a 5' cap (GTP) and a 3' poly-A tail (AAAA); mRNA splicing removes the introns and gives the mature mRNA: 5' cap, protein-coding sequence, 3' poly-A tail, ready to move to cytoplasm. A bracket marks the steps after transcription as post-transcriptional modifications.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.16: Post-transcriptional changes in eukaryotes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.16).

blocks.text: 3- Splicing: The new mRNA is immature because it contains introns (regions of DNA or mRNA that do not code for proteins) and exons (regions of DNA or mRNA which are "expressed" or translated into a protein). mRNA splicing is the process by which introns are removed from the immature mRNA. After splicing, the remaining exons are joined. So, the mature RNA consists of coding segments (gene) only.
